correctness.rationale: The full theorem follows from a k-pebble invariant maintaining pairings and all XOR-zero relations supported on at most k-1 pebbles. Given at most k-1 stationary vertices of rank r, a compatible adjacency signature has a fiber of size 2^(2d-r); if r=k-1, the forbidden span generated by at most k-2 stationary vertices has 2^(k-1)-1 elements, and if r<=k-2, the forbidden span has 2^r elements. For d>=k-1 the fiber strictly exceeds the forbidden set; copying a small linear sum handles all other moves. This sustains an arbitrary-length game. The separator Phi_d uses only d+2 variable names; all d-subsets of a totally isotropic (d+1)-tuple must be independent, which forces their total sum to vanish in ambient rank d, contradicting the chosen odd pairing pattern, while an isotropic (d+1)-frame realizes the pattern in all larger dimensions. The k=1 and k=2 cases follow from atomic patterns and a two-pebble strategy. Programs check dimension-six versus dimension-eight local extensions, every triple in the 15-vertex case, dimension separator and sharp general finite inequalities; they are corroboration rather than the infinite proof.

value.rationale: A complete and sharp all-width, all-depth logical classification for a natural family of finite polar graphs: for k>=3 there are exactly k-1 theories, the stable dimension threshold is k-1, the minimum distinguishing width is d+2 for every d>=2, and the uniform least-representative size is exactly 2^(2(k-1))-1. The fiber-versus-span proof gives a structural explanation why a fixed number of variables permanently loses large symplectic dimensions, while widening the language recovers them. This is not an arbitrary finite census or a routine recomputation of strongly regular graph parameters.
